planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes or container divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil under deciduous shade; Wood Anemone is a spring ephemeral that spreads slowly by shallow rhizomes and is best left undisturbed once established, going fully dormant by midsummer.

directions: Plant rhizomes 2 inches deep in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil beneath deciduous trees where dappled spring sun gives way to summer shade; top-dress with leaf mold each fall to mimic the woodland litter this species evolved with. Wood Anemone is a delicate eastern North American spring ephemeral bearing solitary, star-shaped white to pale pink flowers held just above deeply lobed, five-parted leaves on wiry stems, blooming for a few weeks in early to mid spring before foliage yellows and disappears by early summer. It spreads gradually into loose, airy colonies by thin rhizomes, making an attractive companion for trillium, bloodroot, and other spring ephemerals along a shaded path or woodland garden edge. Because the plant vanishes completely by midsummer, mark its location or interplant with later-emerging ferns and hostas to fill the space it leaves behind.

planting.note: Set out container plants in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; this species tolerates heat and dry shade better than S. hookeriana once its roots are established, making it a strong choice for Gulf South shade gardens.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, and water regularly through the first year to establish a deep root system before easing into its drought-tolerant mature habit. Fragrant Sweet Box is a rounded evergreen shrub with glossy, leathery, willow-like leaves and inconspicuous but powerfully fragrant white flowers produced along the stems in late winter, filling the shade garden with a sweet, honeyed scent when little else is in bloom, followed by showy red berries that ripen to black. Denser and more heat-tolerant than the more commonly planted Himalayan sweet box, it holds up well through hot, humid Gulf Coast summers and is an excellent evergreen backbone for a shaded foundation planting, woodland border, or beneath high tree canopy where deer pressure is a concern, since deer generally avoid it. Prune lightly after flowering only to shape, as it blooms on old wood.

common_name: Pagoda Trout Lily (Yellow Hybrid Trout Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil under deciduous shade; Pagoda is a vigorous hybrid trout lily that naturalizes more readily than the wild species and tolerates a slightly wider range of conditions, though it still prefers cool woodland soil and benefits from a mulch of leaf litter.

directions: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in fall in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained woodland soil, then leave undisturbed to naturalize and multiply into drifts over several years. Pagoda is a robust hybrid trout lily (a cross involving Erythronium tuolumnense and E. californicum) producing mottled, glossy green leaves and nodding, bright sulfur-yellow, reflexed flowers with a brownish base held on wiry stems in early to mid spring, typically two to three blooms per bulb rather than the single flower of most wild species. It is one of the easiest and most vigorous trout lilies for the garden, spreading by offsets to form substantial colonies faster than native species, and pairs beautifully with hellebores, epimedium, and early ferns in a shaded border. Foliage yellows and goes dormant by early summer, so interplant with later-emerging perennials to cover the gap.
sources: Brent and Becky's Bulbs — Erythronium variety notes

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Tardiva blooms several weeks later than most panicle hydrangeas, extending color into early fall, and benefits from afternoon shade in the hottest Gulf South gardens.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants generously to accommodate its large mature size. Tardiva is a classic, tall-growing panicle hydrangea cultivar, dating to the early 20th century, valued for flowering three to four weeks later than most Hydrangea paniculata selections, opening airy, loosely branched white flower panicles composed mostly of small fertile florets with scattered showy sterile florets in late summer that age to a soft pinkish-bronze through fall. Its later bloom time and more open, elegant panicle shape distinguish it from denser modern cultivars like Limelight, making it valued by gardeners who want hydrangea color extending into September and October. Like all panicle hydrangeas it blooms reliably on new wood regardless of pruning timing, so it can be cut back hard in late winter to control size and encourage strong new flowering stems; the large habit also makes it useful as a big-shrub anchor at the back of a mixed border or as a small specimen tree when limbed up.

common_name: Metallicum Japanese Painted Fern (Silvery Metallic Painted Fern)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Metallicum establishes quickly and its distinctive steel-gray coloring intensifies as the fronds mature through the growing season.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and keep soil consistently moist, since painted ferns wilt quickly in dry conditions though they recover once watered. Metallicum is a selection of Japanese painted fern with especially pronounced steel-gray to pewter coloring across the fronds, often with less of the reddish-purple overlay seen in typical Japanese painted fern, giving it a cooler, more silvery cast that reads almost metallic in low woodland light. The low, spreading, slowly clumping habit makes it an excellent front-of-border shade plant or edging along a woodland path, and its color contrasts beautifully with dark-leafed heuchera, hosta, and hardy begonia. Fully hardy and low-maintenance, it dies back to the crown in winter and re-emerges reliably each spring; cut back old fronds in late winter before new growth begins.
